metadata.title: Output costs of education and skill mismatch in OECD countries

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses cross-country microdata from PIAAC (Survey of Adult Skills) for 17 OECD economies, restricted to currently employed respondents. The paper does not report the use of PIAAC sampling weights or any replicate-weight scheme, nor does it name specific weight variables. Because the analysis is a calibrated structural model (not a predictive ML pipeline), the manuscript does not describe complex-survey variance estimation; therefore, readers should treat uncertainty quantification as not documented here. For replication with PIAAC Data Explorer/microdata, analysts should apply the official PIAAC sampling weights for population-representative estimates and use the provided replicate weights (if available) for standard errors, but this paper itself does not specify those steps.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This paper does not estimate cognitive achievement outcomes using PIAAC plausible values; instead, it constructs mismatch measures and calibrates a structural model to match targets derived from PIAAC-based mismatch and wage moments. As a result, PV handling is not applicable to the reported calibration/simulation outputs. The manuscript also does not document a missing-data strategy (e.g., exclusion rules or imputation), which is a reporting gap because PIAAC typically contains item nonresponse.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Uses PIAAC cross-country data collected between 2011 and 2015, and includes only respondents who are currently employed. Mismatch categories are constructed by combining (i) subjective self-assessments of skill/training needs and (ii) objective education/skill classifications based on ISCED attainment (education mismatch) and median literacy/numeracy proficiency (skill mismatch), both computed within 2-digit occupations. Workers are categorized as mismatched only if they are identified as mismatched by both subjective and objective approaches. Wage inputs use gross hourly earnings; for Germany, Sweden, and the US, earnings are reported in deciles and the decile median is assigned to respondents, with trimming of the bottom and top 1% to limit outlier influence.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIAAC (2011-2015) — OECD adult skills (education mismatch calibration targets)
main_findings.target_variable: Output cost of education mismatch (percent change in output when mismatch frictions set to zero)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Average output cost: 2.9% (education mismatch). Cross-country range: 0.4% to 7% of output. Correlation with skill-mismatch output costs: 0.87. Correlation with wage-premium determinant: 0.98 (both education and skill measures). Cut-off: output costs start building when well-matched high-type premium exceeds ~40% (implied threshold around wh/ζwl = 1.4).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIAAC (2011-2015) data for 17 OECD economies, the study leveraged well-matched wage premium, wage cost of under-employment, and wage gain of over-employment to quantify the output cost of education mismatch, finding that eliminating mismatch frictions would raise output by about 2.9% on average (ranging from 0.4% to 7% across countries). This indicates that mismatch policy should focus on reducing wage-related frictions tied to scarcity of well-matched college workers rather than on simply reducing the share of mismatched workers, though the results are model-based calibration rather than causal estimation.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIAAC (2011-2015) — OECD adult skills (skill mismatch calibration targets)
main_findings.target_variable: Output cost of skill mismatch (percent change in output when mismatch frictions set to zero)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Average output cost: 3.8% (skill mismatch). Cross-country range: 1% to 9% of output. Correlation with education-mismatch output costs: 0.87. Correlation with wage-premium determinant: 0.98 (both education and skill measures). Cut-off: output costs start building when well-matched high-type premium exceeds ~40% (implied threshold around wh/ζwl = 1.4).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIAAC (2011-2015) data for 17 OECD economies, the study leveraged well-matched wage premium, wage cost of under-employment, and wage gain of over-employment to quantify the output cost of skill mismatch, finding that eliminating mismatch frictions would raise output by about 3.8% on average (ranging from 1% to 9% across countries). This indicates that strengthening pathways that increase the availability of well-matched skilled workers (and reduce under-employment wage losses) may yield larger macroeconomic gains than targeting mismatch prevalence alone, while the estimates remain dependent on the calibrated structural model.

data.outcome_summary: The paper uses cross-country PIAAC (Survey of Adult Skills) microdata collected between 2011 and 2015 for 17 OECD economies, restricting the sample to currently employed adults. It constructs two mismatch measures—education mismatch (based on ISCED 5B+ attainment within 2-digit occupations combined with subjective self-assessments) and skill mismatch (based on literacy/numeracy proficiency relative to the median within occupations, again combined with subjective mismatch)—and then calibrates a vertical mismatch structural model to match five PIAAC-derived targets (under-/over-employment shares and three relative wage moments). Eliminating the frictions generating mismatch increases output by 2.9% on average for education mismatch and 3.8% for skill mismatch, with substantial cross-country variation (0.4%–7% and 1%–9%, respectively). The two output-cost measures are highly correlated (0.87), and the main determinant is not the mismatch incidence but the wage premium of well-matched workers (correlation 0.98). The study does not report a missing-data strategy or PV handling details because the analysis is calibration/simulation rather than PV-based predictive modeling.
